title: Modelling an OO Application
intro: How to go from a written requirement to a class diagram and a sequence diagram: nouns become classes, verbs become methods, then CRC cards and E/B/C stereotypes. The Blackjack case study runs through it end to end.

cards.title: The modelling steps (slides' order)
cards.body:
Object-oriented modelling copies the way people think: find the **objects** (data plus behaviour) in the requirements, then work out how they interact.
The slides' steps: blue = build the **class diagram**, green = draw the **sequence diagram**, amber = finish and build.

cards.title: Nouns give classes, verbs give methods
cards.body:
Underline the **nouns** in the requirement: these are candidate **classes** (or attributes). Then the **verbs**: these become **responsibilities / methods** or relationships.
In this example, *mentor* and *mentees* are **roles** of Professor and Student, so they become association-end names rather than classes. The noun *results* becomes a `Result` class that links Student and Course.

cards.title: Filtering the candidate classes
cards.body:
List **every** noun first, then eliminate. A noun is dropped when it is:
- the **system itself** (Blackjack = the game)
- a **synonym** (House = Dealer)
- a **plural** of another noun (Players, Cards)
- really an **attribute** (face value, suit, Ace/King/Queen/Jack)
- not needed for this game.
Also ask what you might have **forgotten**. The slides keep **Bet** for future use (then decide it can be added later).

cards.title: Attribute or class?
cards.body:
Some nouns only **describe** another object: a card's face value, a professor's name, a course's `courseName`. These become **attributes**.
A noun becomes a **class** when it has its own data and behaviour, or when it connects other objects. `Result` holds `grade` and `semYr` and links a Student to a Course, so it is a class.

cards.title: Relationships and multiplicities
cards.body:
Phrases in the requirement give the links and the numbers:
"A professor is a mentor to **at least 1** student" gives Professor `1` --- `1..*` Student, with role names mentor / mentee.
"...course results ... which the students have **registered**" gives Student --- Course (register) and a `Result` class tied to a Student and a Course.
keypoints: "at least 1" = `1..*`, "exactly one" = `1`
Multiplicity is written at the FAR end (how many of them)
Role names label the ends: mentor, mentee

cards.title: CRC cards
cards.body:
**CRC = Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators** (Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham, OOPSLA '89). One index card per class:
- **Class name**, plus **superclasses** and **subclasses**
- **Responsibilities** (left): what it knows and does, taken from the verbs
- **Collaborators** (right): the classes it works with to carry out those responsibilities

cards.title: Entity, boundary and control classes
cards.body:
When you identify classes, sort them into three **stereotypes**:
- **Boundary**: the interaction between the actor and the system (UI, forms, device interfaces)
- **Control**: the logic that coordinates and realises a use case
- **Entity**: persistent information the system keeps track of

cards.title: The sequence diagram discovers methods
cards.body: Step 5: walk through one use case (*check mentee result*) as a sequence diagram. **Every arrow that points into a lifeline is a method that class must have.** Add each one to the class diagram (step 6, *enhance class details*).
cards.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
actor Prof as Professor
participant SF as :SelectForm
participant AM as :AppMgr
participant P as professor:Professor
participant S as student:Student
participant R as result:Result
participant C as course:Course
Prof->>SF: select
SF->>AM: showMenteeResults()
AM->>P: getMentees()
loop foreach student
AM->>S: getResults()
loop foreach result
AM->>R: getCourse()
AM->>C: getCourseName()
AM->>R: getGrade()
end
end
AM-->>SF: output
cards.after: Methods discovered: `AppMgr.showMenteeResults()`, `Professor.getMentees()`, `Student.getResults()`, `Result.getCourse()`, `Result.getGrade()`, `Course.getCourseName()`. The `x N` on the slide marks the nested loops: one pass per mentee, then one per result.
keypoints: Arrow into X means X gets a new method
Boundary, then control, then entities: the usual flow
Loops show the 1..* multiplicities in action

cards.title: Case study: Blackjack, summarised
cards.body:
Requirements: one or more players play against the **dealer**. Cards have a face value (Ace = 1 or 11, J/Q/K = 10). Closest to 21 wins, over 21 loses, and a tie at 17 or more is a draw.
After elimination the classes are **Card, Deck, Hand, Dealer, Player** (Bet postponed). The slides' class diagram:

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body:
1. Making **every noun a class**: plurals (Players), synonyms (House), the system itself (Blackjack) and plain values (face value, suit) are not classes.
2. Making **Ace/King/Queen/Jack** subclasses of Card: they are just values of Card's name/value.
3. Putting a responsibility in the wrong class: the class that **holds the data** should do the work (Hand calculates its own value).
4. Mixing up **boundary** (talks to the actor) and **control** (coordinates the use case).
5. Forgetting step 5: the sequence diagram is where missing methods are discovered.
keypoints: Filter nouns before drawing classes
Give the responsibility to the class that holds the data
Boundary faces the actor, control holds the logic, entity holds the data
